newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals - Chinese zinc sales hit Asian premiums.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Chinese zinc sales hit Asian premiums.

text.p: Singapore zinc premiums are coming under pressure with some 20,000 tonnes of Chinese zinc seen heading for the city-state lured by high London Metal Exchange (LME) prices, traders said on Friday.
The traders said the Chinese sales have pushed down Singapore zinc premiums, over LME cash metal, by about $10 a tonne from a week ago.
"The bulk of the (zinc) supplies were sold to a European firm," a Japanese dealer said. "The sale is likely to contribute to the build up of LME stocks in the Singapore warehouse."
But total LME zinc inventories fell by 650 tonnes on Friday. Cash zinc has risen by $80 a tonne over the past week to be quoted at $1,134 a tonne at 0800 GMT on Friday.
Traders attributed the rise to shortcovering and speculative fund buying.
Chinese zinc offers were emerging in the physical market following the recent rally in LME prices which saw three-month metal hit a 23-month at $1,157 a tonne, they said.
"Chinese zinc (exports) have filled the gap in supplies when Russian zinc exports in recent months fell," said one trader.
A European trader said the current market appeared "overbought" and he forsaw a downward correction.
He said growing bearish sentiment in the Far East generated by the jump in Chinese exports will eventually overide the strong European market and cause cash prices to buckle.
"Everyone is worried that levels have topped," he said.
In contrast, the aluminium market is "quite confusing" but most expect prices to stay buoyant.
"There is a lot of near term buying and a lot of forward selling," a trader said. "Most is hand to mouth trade by buyers, while the producers are happy to sell at current levels."
Traders said aluminium demand in Asia was still lacklustre.
The focus in the copper market remained on the steep backwardation, the premium of spot over forward prices.
"There is a shortage of copper in Europe but a lot of quantities are in the Far East," said a trader. "Demand in Asia is weak."

A European dealer added that copper business on the LME next week is expected to be active as Chinese traders "cash in." "We should see some volatile trade. Most players are adopting a wait and see stance," he said.
The copper backwardation on the LME rose to $290/$295 late on Thursday, up from S$234-$238 earlier this week.
Traders noted some speculative buying of lead in Asia which has sparked a jump in Singapore premiums for the metal.
